segments.text: It's launch week. A big newsletter
mentions your product, sign-ups triple
overnight, and someone posts the chart
in the team channel. Everyone feels it.
This is the moment things finally
started working. Four weeks later, you
open the same dashboard and look only at
the people who joined that week. Most of
them haven't come back since their
second day. So, was that product market
fit or just a very good week? It's one
of the most quoted ideas in product
management and one of the most misread.
Marc Andreessen popularized the phrase
in a 2007 essay. He credited the idea to
the investor Andy Rachleff, who traced
it to how Sequoia's founder Don
Valentine picked companies. Andreessen's
definition is short. A good market and a
product that can satisfy it. His real
point was pull. In a great market, the
market pulls the product out of you. The
tempting reading follows. If the market
is pulling, the numbers go up. So, a
growing chart must mean fit. The trouble
is that a growing chart can be produced
in ways that have nothing to do with
fit. You can buy it with ads, borrow it
with a launch, or catch it from a wave
of hype. Branch Out, a professional
networking app built on Facebook, raised
$49 million in total. Its users fell
away anyway, and it relaunched as a
workplace chat app. Sequoia's data
science team calls this a leaky bucket.
Users pour in at the top and simply pass
through. Clubhouse showed the hype
version in early 2021.
It reported more than 10 million weekly
users and a valuation near $4 billion.
Those numbers measured attention, not
whether people would stay.
Two years later, it cut more than half
its staff. Rahul Vohra, the founder of
the email app Superhuman, named the
deeper problem. By the time fit feels
obvious, you already have it. A team
needs a signal that arrives earlier and
one that growth can't fake. The most
reliable one is a retention curve built
cohort by cohort. A cohort is simply
everyone who started in the same week.
You follow that one group forward and
ask at each point what share of them is
still active. Because it's the same
people every time, new sign-ups can't
flatter the line. Left alone, most
curves fall hard. Andrew Chen published
Android data from Quettra in 2015.
The average app lost 77% of its daily
users within 3 days of install. Within
30 days, it had lost 90% and within 90
days, more than 95. Sequoia's team
describes three shapes a curve can take.
A declining curve keeps sliding towards
zero. That's a product without fit. A
flattening curve drops early, then
levels off and holds. A smiling curve
dips and then rises again as people who
left come back. Why does a curve flatten
at all? Everyone in a cohort tries the
product for their own reasons. The
people who don't get lasting value drift
off in the first days or weeks. What
remains is the group that keeps getting
value and once only they're left, the
line stops falling. Brian Balfour's rule
follows directly. If the curve flattens,
you've probably found fit for some
audience.
That last phrase matters. Compare who
stayed with who left. Who they are, when
they joined, where they came from.
If you can't tell them apart, you don't
yet know your market.
In 2020, Lenny Rachitsky and Casey
Winters asked 20 growth leaders what
good retention looks like at 6 months.
For consumer social apps, about 25%
still active counts as good.
For software sold to small businesses,
the figure is closer to 60.
They're practitioners' opinions, so So,
them as rough guides rather than pass
marks.
The weakness of a retention curve is
time. A messaging app can read its curve
within days, but a business tool needs
months of data.
That's why the second instrument exists,
a question you can ask this week.
The growth marketer Sean Ellis asks
users one thing.
How would you feel if you could no
longer use this product?
They answer, very disappointed, somewhat
disappointed, or not disappointed. And
you count the first group. According to
Vora's account, Ellis benchmarked nearly
a hundred startups and found a line at
Companies that struggled almost always
scored below it. Companies with strong
traction almost always scored above.
It's one practitioner's benchmark rather
than a law, but a useful one.
Ellis also chose whom to ask carefully,
people who'd used the product at least
twice in the last two weeks.
Superhuman is the clearest worked
example, and its team started building
By the summer of 2017, it had 14 people
and still hadn't launched.
When Vora finally ran the survey, 22%
said very disappointed, well short of
the line.
Rather than guess, he looked at who
those fans were, founders, managers, and
executives, busy people who live in
their inbox.
Counting only those kinds of users
lifted the score to 33%.
From the fans' own answers, the team
then sketched one imaginary but typical
fan called Nicole.
She reads 1 to 200 emails a day and
prides herself on being responsive.
Why did they love it?
Fans named speed again and again, and
one wrote that they got through their
inbox in half the time.
For someone whose working day happens in
email, speed is the job itself.
The lukewarm users, meanwhile, split
into two quite different groups.
Those who didn't care about speed were
politely set aside.
Those who did were mostly held back by
one thing. There was no mobile app.
So, Vora split the road map down the
middle. Half doubled down on what fans
already loved. The other half removed
what held the near fans back.
Within three quarters, the score nearly
doubled to 58%.
Fit had become something the team could
steer, rather than something it waited
to feel.
Numbers aren't the only evidence.
Ruchitskiy's own test is word of mouth.
Real fit grows with no marketing,
because delighted customers do the
talking.
Paul Graham adds intensity. Build
something a small number of people want
a lot, not something many people want a
little.
There was just one catch, and Vora's own
numbers show it.
Part of that jump from 22 to 33 came
from choosing whom to count.
That's right for finding your core
audience, but misleading as a verdict on
the whole market.
Balfour makes the broader point. Surveys
measure what people say, so they carry
the highest risk of a false positive.
The quieter false positive is who you
happen to measure.
Early adopters forgive things later
users won't, so a score built only on
them will flatter you.
Rockleff's warning covers the louder
ones. Chasing growth before value can
convince you that you found fit.
The second complication is quieter,
because fit isn't permanent.
Then Horowitz listed the belief that you
can't lose it among the myths about fit.
Sean Ellis put it more sharply. A new
competitor can instantly turn a
must-have into a nice-to-have.
Chegg shows how fast that can happen to
an established business.
Students paid a subscription for
human-written homework answers until
chat GPT offered instant personalized
answers for free. They weren't always
right, but they were faster and cheaper.
The loop ran in reverse. Fewer
subscribers, fewer answers, fewer
reasons to subscribe.
Fit can slip from the inside, too.
Vora warned that his score could drop as
Superhuman grew past forgiving early
adopters, so the team rebuilt its road
map every quarter.
So, what should you do with all this?
Before fit, your job is to raise the
flatline and the score, and the advice
is to narrow.
Rackleff says that when something isn't
working, you should change who you're
building for before you change what you
build.
That's exactly what Superhuman did.
To learn why people on that flatline
stay, you have to get close to them.
Paul Graham argues your first picture of
your users is always wrong. The feedback
from working directly with your earliest
users is the best you'll ever get.
Stripe's founders set people up on the
spot. Airbnb's went door-to-door in New
York.
What you shouldn't do yet is pour money
into acquisition.
Before the curve flattens, every new
user goes straight into the leaky
bucket.
Steve Blank called that premature
scaling, and it's one of the most common
ways startups die.
After fit, the curve holds, the fans are
vocal, and spending to grow finally
makes sense. But keep both instruments
running. Survey new users regularly,
watch each new cohort's curve, and treat
a falling score as news rather than
noise.
Go back to launch week and to that chart
in the team channel. The spike was real,
and you should enjoy it. But the
question that matters is how many of
that week's people are still around 2
months later.
If that line has flattened and enough of
them would be very disappointed to lose
you, you found something. If not, it was
simply a very good week.
Next time, we'll sort out who owns these
calls. The product manager, the product
owner, or the project manager?
If this helped, subscribe and tell me
which signal your team trusts today.
